Subject: Deployment mode follow-up: Hosted vs Dedicated vs Private (Lumina Labs)

Hi Claire —

Thanks again for taking the time today. Quick recap and proposed next steps from our call: 

Recap:
- Current setup: majority traffic to OpenAI APIs for prototype; heavier batch/low-latency workloads still running on an internal GPU cluster.
- Goals: reduce per-token cost, improve 95th-percentile latency for inference, and satisfy data residency / audit requirements for PII/logs.
- Traffic profile you mentioned: ~200 QPS steady-state for search/rerank endpoints with spikes up to ~800 QPS during peak runs.
- Constraints: must be able to provide audit logs and key-management that aligns with your compliance team; potential desire to move to VPC-hosted control plane.

What we recommend (high-level):
- Hosted API (fastest to ship): lowest friction for proof-of-concept. Good for non-sensitive workloads and early product launches.
- Dedicated capacity: reserved GPU pools for predictable throughput and lower unit cost; keeps data isolated in a tenant-specific environment in our cloud offering. Meets most enterprise requirements with SLA.
- Private (VPC / on-prem): full control plane in your VPC or on-prem. Best for strict data residency and regulatory requirements but involves a longer integration and provisioning timeline.

Next steps I propose:
1) Tech deep-dive with David to map your model sizes, sequence lengths, and latency SLOs so we can size Dedicated pools and quantify batching gains.
2) I’ll send a concise deployment comparison and a migration playbook that covers: switching from OpenAI API calls to Redwood routing, adapting client SDKs, and a phased rollout plan from Hosted -> Dedicated -> Private if needed.
3) Provide cost ballparks for Dedicated vs Private along with an estimated timeline.

I’ve attached a short deployment comparison and a starter migration map for your review. If you want, we can target a tech call the week of Aug 18.

Thanks — looking forward to continuing the conversation.

—

Hey Claire — great, thanks for confirming availability. I attached a short matrix and a migration playbook that should help when you explain tradeoffs to your security and infra teams. Key points below (high level):

Hosted API:
- Pros: fastest time-to-value, no infra management, automatic model updates.
- Cons: less control over keys unless you choose customer-managed KMS integration; not ideal for strict data residency.
- Use case: dev/proof-of-concept and non-PII workloads.

Dedicated Capacity:
- Pros: tenant-isolated GPU pools, predictable throughput, lower per-token cost at commit levels, Redwood-managed control plane with SLA.
- Cons: provisioning lead time (1–3 weeks depending on commit), requires network allowlists and optionally VPC peering.
- Use case: production workloads that need predictable performance and isolation without full on-prem rollout.

Private (VPC / On-prem):
- Pros: full control, in-VPC control plane, KMS/HSM options, audit logs forwarded to your systems, meets strict regulatory constraints.
- Cons: longest lead time (4–8+ weeks depending on infra), higher ops involvement.

Ballpark monthly cost ranges (very rough estimates based on the traffic you described and typical model profiles):
- Hosted: $8k–$18k (variable, pay-as-you-go)
- Dedicated (reserved): $22k–$45k (depending on commit and model footprint)
- Private (VPC/on-prem): $40k+ (higher up-front integration; Opex + possible infra costs)

Migration approach we recommend (phased):
1) Prototype on Hosted to validate prompts and evaluation metrics (2–4 weeks).
2) Move latency/throughput-critical endpoints to Dedicated for predictable SLOs; use prefix/KV caching to reduce token costs (2–3 weeks after sizing).
3) If required by compliance, transition to Private with data plane in your VPC and KMS integration (4–8+ weeks).

I’ve attached: redwood-deployment-comparison.pdf (matrix) and lumina-migration-map.xlsx (high-level timeline + owners). I’ve CC’d David to coordinate the tech call — he’ll walk through sizing and kernel/quantization tradeoffs.

Let me know if you want the breakdown in a slide-friendly format for your security review; we can also include our SOC2 artifacts.

—
